The audio signal further comprises depth-position data indicative of a target depth position for the first audio object. outputs.L2: An audio-processing device includes a receiver (101) configured to obtain an audio signal containing sound data for at least one audio object linked to a three-dimensional image. The signal further carries depth-location information specifying an intended depth for that audio object. A determination unit (107) identifies the visual depth interval supported by a target 3D display used to show the image. In particular, the identified interval may correspond to the range within which the display can reproduce objects accurately. The mapping unit (109) may then adjust the locations of the audio-object sound sources so that they coincide with the depth locations of their associated visual objects on the 3D display.
outputs.L3:
The apparatus receives an audio signal containing audio data for at least one audio object associated with a three-dimensional image. The audio signal also includes depth-position data specifying a target depth for the audio object.

A determiner identifies the visual rendering depth range supported by the target three-dimensional display. Based on this range, a mapper converts the audio object’s target depth into an appropriate rendering depth for the display. The apparatus can then adjust the perceived position of the audio source so that it aligns with the displayed depth position of the corresponding visual object. This coordination between audio and visual rendering improves spatial consistency and creates a more immersive three-dimensional viewing experience.
outputs.L4:
An audio signal processing apparatus is configured to coordinate the perceived position of audio sources with the displayed positions of corresponding objects in a three-dimensional image. The apparatus receives audio-object data representing one or more audio objects, together with target depth information indicating the intended depth position of each object within a three-dimensional scene. The audio-object data may include an audio signal and metadata identifying a desired spatial position, such as horizontal, vertical, and depth coordinates.

The apparatus also obtains information concerning the visual depth range that can be accurately reproduced by a target display device. This range may depend on characteristics of the display, including its physical configuration, stereoscopic or multiview capabilities, viewing geometry, and supported disparity limits. The visual depth range can identify the nearest and farthest positions at which visual objects can be rendered without excessive distortion, discomfort, or loss of depth accuracy.

Using the target depth information and the determined visual depth range, the apparatus maps the intended depth position of each audio object to a corresponding reproduced depth position. For example, when the intended scene depth extends beyond the range supported by the display, the apparatus may scale, compress, clip, or otherwise transform the audio-object depth coordinates so that they correspond to the depths at which associated visual objects are actually displayed. The mapping may be linear or nonlinear and may preserve selected reference positions, such as the display plane, a primary subject position, or a preferred listening location.

The mapped depth positions are then used to generate, modify, or render spatial audio signals. Depending on the playback system, this processing may involve adjusting speaker gains, delays, filters, reverberation, binaural cues, or other spatial-audio parameters. Each audio source is thereby perceived at a depth that more closely matches the rendered depth of its corresponding visual object.

By basing audio positioning on the target display’s effective visual depth range rather than solely on the original scene coordinates, the apparatus reduces discrepancies between auditory and visual localization. This improves audiovisual spatial consistency and provides a more coherent and immersive three-dimensional viewing and listening experience across displays having different depth-rendering capabilities.

### The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the most common words in the English language. Although it contains only three letters, it plays an essential role in communication. As the definite article, “the” identifies a particular person, place, object, or idea. For example, saying “the book” refers to a specific book, while “a book” could mean any book.

This small word also helps create clarity and shared understanding. Phrases such as “the sun,” “the internet,” and “the future” point to concepts that people recognize as unique or familiar. Often unnoticed, “the” demonstrates how even the simplest words can give language structure, precision, and meaning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent abstract for an audio signal processing apparatus that maps the depth position of an audio object to the rendering depth range of a 3D display.
counterfactuals.output: An audio signal processing apparatus includes an input interface configured to obtain audio object data specifying a depth position of an audio object, and display information identifying a rendering depth range of a three-dimensional display. A mapping processor maps the depth position of the audio object from an audio coordinate space to a corresponding position within the rendering depth range of the three-dimensional display. The mapping may be based on a normalized depth value, a nonlinear mapping function, or one or more display-dependent depth constraints. An audio renderer generates an output audio signal such that the audio object is perceived at a spatial depth corresponding to the mapped position. By coordinating perceived audio depth with visual depth available to the three-dimensional display, the apparatus improves spatial alignment between rendered audio objects and displayed visual objects across displays having different depth-rendering capabilities.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention that receives object-based audio with depth metadata and adjusts virtual sound-source positions so they match corresponding visual objects on a three-dimensional display.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention is an audiovisual rendering system that spatially aligns object-based audio with imagery shown on a three-dimensional display.

The system receives:

- Separate audio objects, such as dialogue, music, or sound effects;
- Metadata identifying each audio object’s position, including depth; and
- Information describing the positions of corresponding visual objects in the displayed 3D scene.

A processor maps the audio-coordinate system to the display-coordinate system and compares each audio object’s intended location with the apparent location of its associated visual object. It then adjusts the virtual sound-source coordinates—particularly depth, but also horizontal and vertical position when needed—so the sound appears to originate from the visual object. The adjustment may account for display size, stereoscopic disparity, viewer position, head tracking, and the speaker or headphone configuration.

The corrected audio-object positions are supplied to a spatial renderer, which generates loudspeaker feeds or binaural headphone signals. Thus, for example, speech from a character appearing in front of the screen is perceived as coming from that character’s 3D location rather than from the screen plane or a fixed speaker.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an abstract for a patent concerning audiovisual depth alignment, including receipt of audio data and target depth information, determination of a 3D display’s usable depth range, and remapping of audio-source positions to match displayed visual objects.
counterfactuals.output: A method, system, and non-transitory computer-readable medium for audiovisual depth alignment are disclosed. Audio data associated with one or more audio sources and target depth information indicating intended spatial positions of corresponding visual objects are received. A usable depth range of a three-dimensional display is determined based on display characteristics, operating conditions, viewer information, or combinations thereof. When a target depth is outside the usable depth range or differs from a depth at which a corresponding visual object is displayed, the position of the associated audio source is remapped to an adjusted depth within the usable depth range. The remapping may preserve relative depth relationships among multiple audiovisual objects and may account for display clipping, depth compression, viewer location, and audio-rendering constraints. Spatial audio output is generated using the remapped audio-source positions such that perceived audio locations are aligned with the displayed visual objects. The alignment may be updated dynamically in response to changes in content, display configuration, or viewing conditions.
